title: Exploratory Data Analysis & Visualisation
blurb: Tests whether you can read a distribution, pick the right chart, interpret correlations without over-reading them, and spot confounding and data snooping before they reach a model.

ideas.title: Univariate analysis: centre, spread, skew and outliers
Choosing the right chart for the question
ideas.ref: §9.2.2, Quick Reference: Plot Type Decision Guide

ideas.title: Correlation: Pearson, Spearman, redundancy and causation
Summary statistics hide shape: always visualise

questions.prompt: The chapter's EDA progression ends with "What surprised me?". Why is that question asked last?
options: Recognising a surprise needs the baseline the first four questions build
Asking it earlier would leak information about the test set into feature choices
A surprise can only be confirmed once a baseline model has been trained on the data
Surprises matter least to the eventual model, so they are left until the end
questions.explanation: You cannot recognise a surprise until you know what "normal" looks like for this dataset. The first four questions (what do I have, each variable alone, variables together, variables against the target) build that baseline. The chapter calls it the important question, so "matters least" has it backwards.

questions.prompt: Which pair of summary statistics is **robust** to a handful of extreme values?
options: Mean and IQR
Median and standard deviation
Mean and standard deviation
Median and IQR
questions.explanation: The median and the interquartile range ($Q_3 - Q_1$) depend only on the middle of the sorted data, so a few extreme values barely move them. The mean and the standard deviation both use every value's size, so one huge value can pull them a long way. The mixed pairs each include one non-robust statistic.

questions.prompt: You want to see whether a **numeric** variable's distribution shifts across the levels of a **categorical** variable. Which chart does the chapter recommend?
options: A stacked bar chart of counts per category
Box or violin plots, one per category
A scatter plot of the numeric variable against the category codes
A correlation heatmap of all numeric columns
questions.explanation: For numeric against categorical, box or violin plots per category show whether the distribution moves. If it does, the categorical variable carries information. Scatter plots are for two numeric variables. Stacked bars are for two categorical ones. A Pearson heatmap needs numeric pairs.

questions.prompt: When should you prefer Spearman correlation over Pearson correlation?
options: When you want evidence that one variable causes the other
When the relationship is monotonic but not linear
When both variables are categorical
When the relationship is U-shaped
questions.explanation: Pearson measures linear association. Spearman measures monotonic association (consistently up, or consistently down), linear or not. A U-shape is not monotonic, so Spearman misses it too. Neither coefficient says anything about causation.

questions.prompt: On Titanic, age has a marginal correlation of only $-0.08$ with survival. What did the chapter's multivariate step show?
options: The weak correlation is an artefact of the 19.9% of ages that are missing
Age is mostly a proxy for fare, so the two features are redundant for modelling
Holding class fixed reveals a "children first" effect in 1st and 2nd class
Age has no relationship with survival once nulls are imputed, so drop it
questions.explanation: Splitting age by both class and survival revealed a "children first" effect concentrated in 1st and 2nd class. It is invisible in the marginal correlation and only appears once class is held fixed. Dropping age on the marginal number is exactly the mistake multivariate analysis exists to prevent.

questions.prompt: What does Anscombe's quartet demonstrate?
options: Boxplots are more informative than histograms for small datasets
Outliers should be removed before summary statistics are computed
Identical summary statistics can hide very different shapes
Pearson correlation is always misleading on small samples
questions.explanation: The four datasets share the same summary numbers but look completely different when plotted: a line, a curve, a line with one outlier, and a vertical cluster plus one leverage point. The lesson is to visualise even when the summary numbers look informative. It does not say correlation is always misleading, only that it cannot tell these shapes apart.

questions.prompt: What is **data snooping** in the sense used in this chapter?
options: Letting EDA on the full dataset, test rows included, shape later choices
Inspecting `df.head()` instead of `df.sample()`, so only early rows are seen
Reading a customer's data without formal sign-off from the data owner
Looking at the target variable during EDA, before any model is trained
questions.explanation: Data snooping means learning so much about the dataset, including the test set, that later feature choices are tuned to data the model should never have seen. Looking at the target is not snooping. The chapter calls feature-against-target the most important bivariate check. The issue is which rows you look at, not which column.

questions.prompt: EDA is observing, feature engineering is transforming. Which of these is an **EDA output** rather than a feature engineering step?
options: `age` nulls filled with the median age within each passenger class
`embarked` one-hot encoded into three indicator columns for the model
A new column `log_fare = np.log1p(df['fare'])` added to the training frame
A note that `fare` is right-skewed, so a log transform is worth testing
questions.explanation: The chapter says the most valuable EDA output is a written list of hypotheses and surprises, which then informs Chapter 14. The note records an observation and a hypothesis. The other three change the data, which is feature engineering (or cleaning), even when EDA suggested them.

questions.prompt: An exam's scores have a mean of 61 and a median of 72. What does this suggest about the distribution?
options: A symmetric distribution with two peaks
Positive (right) skew: a long tail of high scores pulls the mean up
Negative (left) skew: a tail of low scores pulls the mean down
A symmetric distribution with heavier tails than a normal
questions.explanation: The mean is sensitive to extreme values, the median is not. The mean sits well below the median, so something is dragging it down: a long left tail of low scores. That is negative skew, and `series.skew()` would be below 0. The right-skew option has the direction reversed. A symmetric shape would put mean and median close together. A histogram with KDE would confirm the shape.

questions.prompt: A telco customer asks whether **contract type** (3 levels) is associated with **payment method** (4 levels). Which chart answers this?
options: A Pearson correlation heatmap of the label-encoded columns
A cross-tabulation shown as a stacked bar chart or pivot heatmap
A histogram of payment method with a KDE overlay
A scatter plot of contract type against payment method, one dot per customer
questions.explanation: Two categorical variables call for a cross-tab, shown as a stacked bar or pivot heatmap. It shows whether knowing one tells you something about the other. Label-encoding categories and taking Pearson is the tempting trap: the integer codes have an arbitrary order, so the coefficient is meaningless.
questions.ref: §9.2.2, Quick Reference: Plot Type Decision Guide

questions.prompt:
What does this code print?

```python
import pandas as pd
x = pd.Series([1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6])
y = x ** 3
print(round(x.corr(y), 2), round(x.corr(y, method='spearman'), 2))
```
questions.explanation: $y = x^3$ is strictly increasing, so the ranks of $y$ match the ranks of $x$ exactly and Spearman is **1.0**. Pearson measures how close the points are to a straight line. The cubic curve bends, so Pearson is below 1, at **0.94**. The `1.0 1.0` option assumes Pearson also detects any perfect relationship. It only rewards linear ones. (Pandas needs SciPy installed for `method='spearman'`.)

questions.prompt:
How many **off-diagonal scatter panels** does this call draw?

```python
sns.pairplot(df, vars=['tenure', 'monthly_spend', 'tickets', 'logins'], hue='churned')
```

Give an integer.
questions.explanation: A pairplot draws a $4 \times 4$ grid for 4 variables: 16 panels. The 4 on the diagonal show each variable's own distribution, split by `churned`. The other $16 - 4 =$ **12** are scatter plots, one for every ordered pair. Each unordered pair appears twice, mirrored across the diagonal. Answering 6 counts unordered pairs only.

questions.prompt: `df['latency_ms'].describe()` shows mean 200, median 198 and std 50. A colleague concludes that latency is "roughly normal, one peak, no transform needed". What is the right next step?
options: Draw a boxplot, which will show whether there is more than one peak
Apply the z-score rule to remove values beyond 3 standard deviations
Accept the conclusion, since a mean close to the median proves a single peak
Plot a histogram with KDE, since the summary cannot rule out two peaks
questions.explanation: Mean close to median suggests symmetry, not a single peak. Two server pools at 150 ms and 250 ms would give similar numbers. The chapter's common mistake is running `.describe()` and stopping there. A boxplot is the tempting answer, but boxplots show quartiles, not shape, and hide bimodality entirely.

questions.prompt: Which workflow avoids data snooping?
options: Run full EDA on all rows but ignore the target column, then split
Split first, then run full EDA on the training partition only
Run full EDA on all rows, then split, since EDA does not fit any model yet
Run EDA on the test partition, since it best reflects unseen data
questions.explanation: Split first, then explore only the training data, and treat the test set as if it does not exist until final evaluation. "EDA does not fit a model" is the tempting argument, but thresholds, buckets and "this feature looks predictive" judgements are still choices tuned to the rows you looked at. Hiding the target does not help, since those choices do not need labels to be biased.

questions.prompt: A first profiling pass (Procedure 9.1) on a new fraud dataset finds: `signup_date` has dtype `object`, 3% of rows are exact duplicates, and the target `is_fraud` is 0.8% positive. Select ALL items that belong in the written EDA summary handed to later stages.
options: Log-transform `signup_date` to reduce its skew
Remove the fraud rows as outliers, since they are under 1% of the data
Accuracy will be misleading at a 0.8% positive rate, so plan imbalance-aware metrics
Check whether the duplicates are true repeat events or a join bug before removing them
`signup_date` must be parsed to a datetime before any date features are built
questions.explanation: The three correct items are findings plus the decisions they suggest, which is what EDA hands to Chapter 14. The imbalance note mirrors the Titanic target analysis. Duplicates are something to investigate, not delete by reflex. A date stored as text needs parsing first. Treating the rare positive class as outliers would throw away the very cases the model must learn. A log transform makes no sense for a date column.

questions.prompt:
Using the IQR rule from Listing 9.6 with $k = 1.5$ and pandas' default quantile method (linear interpolation), what is the **upper fence** for this sample?

```python
s = pd.Series([12, 15, 14, 10, 18, 16, 13, 95, 11, 17])
```

Give a number to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation: Sorted: 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 18, 95 ($n = 10$). Pandas places quantile $p$ at position $(n-1)p$ (0-indexed). $Q_1$ sits at $9 \times 0.25 = 2.25$, between 12 and 13, so $Q_1 = 12.25$. $Q_3$ sits at $6.75$, between 16 and 17, so $Q_3 = 16.75$. $\text{IQR} = 4.5$. Upper fence $= 16.75 + 1.5 \times 4.5 =$ **23.50**. Only 95 is flagged. It might be a typo for 9.5 or a real extreme case. Investigate before deleting.

questions.prompt: An analyst draws `sns.scatterplot(data=df, x='session_length', y='basket_value')` on 2 million web sessions. The plot is a solid dark blob and shows no structure. What is the best diagnosis and fix?
options: No relationship exists: a correlation heatmap will confirm it
Overplotting: set a low `alpha=` or plot a random sample of rows
The histogram bin width is too wide: reduce the number of bins
The variables need Spearman correlation instead of a scatter plot
questions.explanation: The Plot Type Comparison lists overplotting with large N as the scatter plot's weakness, and the fix as transparency (`alpha=`) or sampling. A blob is a rendering problem, not evidence of no relationship. Bin width belongs to histograms. Swapping the chart for one coefficient throws away the shape the scatter plot exists to show.

questions.prompt: Across a retailer's 120 stores, staff training hours correlate at $r = 0.71$ with monthly sales. The customer proposes mandating 40 extra training hours in every store to lift sales. Which response is most defensible from EDA alone?
options: The correlation is strong, so training explains about 71% of the variation in sales
The correlation is too weak to act on, since only $r$ above 0.95 is meaningful
Switch to Spearman. If it is also high, the causal effect is confirmed
Not yet. Store size could drive both, so compare within store-size groups
questions.explanation: Correlation measures association, not causation. Large stores may have both more training hours and more sales. Holding store size fixed is the multivariate check that exposes this. The 71% option confuses $r$ with $r^2$ (which would be about 50%) and still says nothing about cause. The 0.95 figure is the chapter's redundancy threshold between two features, not a significance cutoff. Spearman changes the kind of association measured, not whether it is causal.

questions.prompt:
A SaaS customer compares 12-month churn for two plans, split by customer segment:

| Segment | Plan A customers | Plan A churned | Plan B customers | Plan B churned |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SMB | 800 | 160 | 200 | 50 |
| Enterprise | 200 | 10 | 800 | 48 |

What is Plan A's **overall** churn rate minus Plan B's overall churn rate? Give percentage points to 1 d.p.
questions.explanation: Plan A overall: $(160 + 10)/1000 = 17.0\%$. Plan B overall: $(50 + 48)/1000 = 9.8\%$. The difference is **7.2** points, so Plan B looks far better. Now look within segments. SMB: A $= 160/800 = 20\%$, B $= 50/200 = 25\%$. Enterprise: A $= 10/200 = 5\%$, B $= 48/800 = 6\%$. Plan A has the **lower** churn in both segments. The overall gap comes from Plan A's customers being mostly SMB, the high-churn segment. This reversal is Simpson's paradox.

questions.prompt:
What does this code print?

```python
import pandas as pd
x = pd.Series([5, 5, 5, 5, 15])
y = pd.Series([3, 5, 4, 6, 12])
print(round(x.corr(y), 2), x[:4].corr(y[:4]))
```
questions.explanation: With all five points: $\bar x = 7$, $\bar y = 6$, $S_{xy} = 60$, $S_{xx} = 80$, $S_{yy} = 50$, so $r = 60/\sqrt{80 \times 50} =$ **0.95**. Drop the last point and $x$ is constant (variance 0), so the correlation is undefined and pandas returns `nan`. It is not 0. One high-leverage point creates the entire strong correlation, like panel D in Figure 9.1. Only a plot shows this.

questions.prompt: A team ran EDA on all 50,000 rows before splitting 80/20. Select ALL decisions below that are contaminated by data snooping.
options: Capping `fare` at 400 because a histogram of all rows showed a gap above that value
Checking after the split that the training partition's target rate matches the original 38%
Choosing `income` as a promising feature after seeing its separation by target on all rows
Bucketing `embarked` levels with fewer than 20 rows (counted on all rows) into `other`
questions.explanation: Each of the first three is a threshold, bucket or feature judgement made with the test rows in view. The chapter names exactly these kinds of choices. They are tuned to the rows that will later evaluate the model, which inflates its apparent generalisation. Checking the training partition's target rate after the split only confirms the split is balanced. It shapes no threshold, bucket or feature choice, so it is not snooping.

questions.prompt: A column holds nine values: eight are `1` and one is `100` (a clear data-entry error). Listing 9.6's `zscore_outliers` uses `scipy.stats.zscore`, which divides by the population standard deviation (`ddof=0`). What is the z-score of the value 100? Give a number to 2 d.p.
questions.explanation: Mean $= (8 + 100)/9 = 12$. Deviations: $-11$ (eight times) and $88$. Population variance $= (8 \times 11^2 + 88^2)/9 = 8712/9 = 968$, so $\sigma \approx 31.11$. $z = 88 / 31.11 =$ **2.83**. The rule with threshold 3 flags nothing. This is no accident. With $n$ values and `ddof=0`, no $|z|$ can exceed $\sqrt{n-1}$, which is $\sqrt{8} \approx 2.83$ here. The outlier inflates the very standard deviation used to judge it, so a z-score threshold of 3 cannot fire for $n < 10$. At $n = 10$ the maximum is exactly 3, and only floating-point noise can push it over. The IQR rule has $Q_1 = Q_3 = 1$ and flags the 100 at once. In small samples, prefer the IQR rule.
questions.ref: Procedure 9.5, Quick Reference: Outlier Detection Methods

questions.prompt:
What does this code print, and what does it show?

```python
import pandas as pd
x = pd.Series([-3, -2, -1, 0, 1, 2, 3])
y = x ** 2
print(round(x.corr(y), 2), round(x.corr(y, method='spearman'), 2))
```
options: `1.0 1.0`: $y$ is a deterministic function of $x$, so both coefficients are perfect
`0.0 0.0`: $y$ is independent of $x$ over this range
`0.0 0.0`: both miss a perfect U-shaped dependence that a scatter plot shows
`0.0 1.0`: Pearson misses the curve but Spearman catches any non-linear relationship
questions.explanation: The points are symmetric about $x = 0$, so the linear association is exactly 0. Spearman is 0 too. The ranks of $y$ are also symmetric in $x$, and a U-shape is not monotonic. The chapter's fix of switching to Spearman only works for monotonic curves. The tempting `0.0 1.0` assumes Spearman handles any non-linearity. Reading `0.0 0.0` as independence is the classic error: $y$ is fully determined by $x$.

questions.prompt: Every value in an `income` column is positive, and the column is heavily right-skewed. You replace it with `np.log(income)`. Select ALL statements that must be true.
options: The IQR rule ($k = 1.5$) may now flag a different set of customers
The Pearson correlation between income and `tenure` is unchanged
The mean of `log(income)` equals the log of the mean income
The Spearman correlation between income and `tenure` is unchanged
questions.explanation: Log is strictly increasing on positive values, so every customer's rank is unchanged and Spearman, which uses ranks, is unchanged. Pearson depends on the actual values and generally changes. The IQR fences are computed on the new scale, where the long right tail is pulled in, so points that were upper outliers may no longer be flagged and low values may become flagged. The mean does not commute with log: the mean of the logs is at most the log of the mean, with equality only when every value is the same.

questions.prompt:
A different SaaS customer reports 12-month churn for two plans, split by segment:

| Segment | Plan A customers | Plan A churned | Plan B customers | Plan B churned |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| SMB | 900 | 270 | 300 | 105 |
| Enterprise | 100 | 4 | 700 | 35 |

Their VP says: "Plan B churns far less overall. Move every new customer onto Plan B." What is the most defensible response?
options: Yes, but only for SMB customers, since that is where the overall gap arises
No. Plan A churns less in each segment. B only wins overall through its mix
No. Plan A is better overall once the two segment rates are averaged equally
Yes. The overall rate is what the business experiences, so it is the right comparison
questions.explanation: Overall, Plan A churns $274/1000 = 27.4\%$ and Plan B $140/1000 = 14.0\%$, so B looks far better. Segment confounds that comparison. SMB customers churn far more on either plan, and Plan A has three times as many of them. Compared like for like, Plan A is lower in both segments (30% vs 35%, 4% vs 5%). Moving SMB customers to Plan B would, on this evidence, raise their churn. "Overall is what the business experiences" is tempting, but it answers a different question from "which plan is better for a given customer". The equal-average option reaches the right verdict by the wrong route. Averaging segment rates is not an overall rate.

bookExercises.prompt: List the five questions this chapter's EDA progression asks, in order, and explain in one sentence why "what surprises me?" is placed last rather than first.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: The five questions, in order: (1) what do I have (shape, types, nulls, duplicates); (2) what does each variable look like alone (distributions, outliers, skew); (3) how do variables relate to each other (correlations, conditional distributions); (4) how do variables relate to the target; (5) what surprises me. "What surprises me?" is placed last because it can only be answered after the first four questions have established a baseline of expectations. You can't recognise a surprise until you know what "normal" looks like for this specific dataset.

bookExercises.prompt: A dataset's `age` column has a mean of 29.7 and a median of 24.0. What does the gap between them suggest about the distribution's shape, and which single chart would confirm it?
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A mean of 29.7 against a median of 24.0 means the mean is pulled upward relative to the median, indicating a right-skewed (positive skew) distribution, a small number of unusually old passengers/customers/etc. stretching the upper tail. A histogram with a KDE overlay (Listing 9.4) would confirm the shape directly and show whether the skew is mild or extreme.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 9.2 as a starting point, run it against a dataset of your choosing and report which columns, if any, have more than 10% missing values.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Answer depends on the dataset chosen; the deliverable is a `quick_profile()` run and a reported list of columns exceeding 10% missing, following the exact output format of Listing 9.2. For example, on the Titanic dataset used in this chapter, only `deck` (77.2%) and `age` (19.9%) exceed that threshold.

bookExercises.prompt: Using Listing 9.8's grouping pattern, compute the Titanic survival rate broken down by `embarked` instead of `sex`, and state whether the spread across categories looks large enough to be a useful feature.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: `df.groupby('embarked')['survived'].mean()` on the Titanic dataset returns roughly 55% survival for passengers who embarked at Cherbourg (C), 39% at Queenstown (Q), and 34% at Southampton (S). The spread (~20 points between C and S) is large enough to be worth investigating as a feature, though it is confounded with class: Cherbourg passengers were disproportionately 1st class, so some of this apparent effect is really the class/fare effect from Listing 9.8 showing through a correlated variable.

bookExercises.prompt: Reproduce Listing 9.5's "near-redundant pair" check on the Titanic numeric features (`survived`, `pclass`, `age`, `sibsp`, `parch`, `fare`) and confirm whether any pair exceeds the 0.9 threshold.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Running Listing 9.5's near-redundant-pair check on `survived`, `pclass`, `age`, `sibsp`, `parch`, `fare` finds no pair above the 0.9 threshold. The strongest pairwise correlation among the features (excluding the target) is `pclass`/`fare` at roughly $-0.55$, well below the redundancy cutoff. This dataset has essentially no redundant numeric feature pairs, so no columns need to be dropped purely on multicollinearity grounds.

bookExercises.prompt: The chapter found that age's marginal correlation with `survived` was only $-0.08$, yet a clear "children first" effect appeared once the data was split by class. Propose one other pair of Titanic features where you'd expect a similar Simpson's-paradox-style effect, and explain your reasoning before checking it.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: A plausible candidate is `fare` split by `pclass` and `survived` jointly: the marginal correlation between `fare` and `survived` (0.26) is real but could hide a stronger within-class effect, since fare varies enormously within 1st class (from a low-end 1st-class ticket to the most expensive suites). A passenger paying a high fare within a low-status class might show a much bigger survival boost than the marginal correlation suggests. The general pattern to watch for: any feature whose marginal relationship to the target looks weak but which is known to vary systematically with a third, stronger predictor (here, class) is a Simpson's-paradox candidate.

bookExercises.prompt: A colleague proposes running full EDA, including test-set rows, before splitting the data, arguing "we're just looking, not modelling yet." Using this chapter's data-snooping discussion, write two or three sentences explaining what could go wrong.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Running EDA on the full dataset including test rows means any pattern discovered (an outlier threshold, a "this feature looks predictive" judgment, a bucketing scheme for rare categories) has implicitly been chosen with knowledge of the test set's actual values. Even without directly touching the labels, decisions like "drop rows where fare > 400" or "bucket embarked's rare category into 'other'" become choices tuned to the specific data points that will later be used to evaluate the model, inflating the model's apparent generalisation performance. The fix is to split first, then run full EDA only on the training partition, treating the test set as if it doesn't exist until final evaluation.

bookExercises.prompt: Read about Anscombe's quartet (or its modern descendant, the "Datasaurus Dozen"). Pick one of the four Anscombe datasets and describe, without plotting it, what summary statistics alone would have told you, and what they would have hidden.
bookExercises.modelAnswer: Discussion only, no single answer. Each of Anscombe's four datasets shares an identical mean, variance, and Pearson correlation coefficient (~0.816), so summary statistics alone would report the same numbers for all four and suggest the same linear relationship strength. What they hide: one dataset is a genuine linear relationship with noise; one is a clean non-linear (quadratic-like) curve that Pearson's linear correlation badly misrepresents; one is a near-perfect linear relationship broken by a single outlier that shifts the fitted line; and one is a vertical cluster of points entirely determined by one high-leverage outlier. Only plotting each one reveals which of these four very different stories the identical statistics were describing.
